scenario: AITA for telling people there is no end credit scene? | IF YOU CARE ABOUT END CREDIT SCENES LIKE THESE PEOPLE DONT READ I GUESS So, I have been working at a movie theater for a summer job, and my movie theater has ushers, but ushers at our theater don’t rip people’s tickets, they just clean the theaters. So that’s what I’ve been doing recently on my shifts and it’s pretty laid back and easy. So ushers get a door sheet, and it has what theaters to go to in an order so you can clean each theater after everyone gets out efficiently. And I had Dark Phoenix and another movie to clean at the same time. It’s super slow on weekdays so it’s not a big deal. But I knew the other movie besides Dark Phoenix was pretty crowded so I wanted to be as efficient as possible. So when I walked into Dark Phoenix, and the credits were rolling, there was 4 sets of people still in the theater presumably waiting for the end credit scene like most super hero movies have these days. So, to help them out (in my mind I guess) and myself out to clean the theater faster, I told them “hey guys, you don’t have to wait around there’s no end credit scene.” I’ve done this many times with no issues but this couple in this showing had an issue. They got up from their seat and yelled at me for “ruining their movie going experience” and wanted to speak to a manager. So I call a manger to the theater and they tell the manger that I was rude for spoiling that there was no end credit scene and they complained also that I was shining a flash light as well. I told my manager that last part was false but I didn’t see an issue with telling them as it saved them time. My manager told the couple we were sorry and he gave them a free movie pass. Once they left, my manager told me to just stop telling people about how there’s no end credit scene. So Reddit, AITA for telling people there’s no end credit scene or was this just a weird couple?

(0/1 = Yes, but with context)** **1 = Wrong (or at least unprofessional)** **0 = Not wrong, but risky/depends on context** **I’d lean toward 0.5 (a mix), but closer to 1 for these reasons:** #### **Arguments for "Not Wrong" (0):** - **Efficiency & Service Intent**: You were trying to help—both the customers (who might have been waiting unnecessarily) and yourself (to clean faster). Some people *do* know this, and it’s not like you’re lying. - **Common Knowledge**: Many superhero movies (especially Marvel/DC) have had missing end credits for years. It’s not a secret—just a frustration for some fans. #### **Arguments for "Wrong" (1):** - **Customer Experience > Efficiency**: Theaters exist to provide an *experience*, not just a service. Even if the credits were missing, the couple felt their *entire* movie-going experience was ruined by the interruption. That’s a valid complaint. - **Unprofessional Boundary**: Even if your intent was good, you *did* break the "don’t spoil the experience" rule. Some customers take this very personally, especially if they’re fans who *expect* the credits. - **Manager’s Decision**: Your manager told you to stop doing it, which means the theater’s policy is to *not* do this. Following workplace rules is important, even if you disagree with them. - **Potential for Escalation**: You could’ve been in a worse situation—what if the couple had been more aggressive, or if the manager had been stricter? Even if it was "just a weird couple," it’s better to avoid the risk. #### **Why the Couple Reacted So Strongly:** - **Fan Culture**: Many movie-goers (especially for superhero films) *expect* end credits and see them as part of the experience. Skipping them can feel like a betrayal. - **Perceived Rudeness**: Even if you meant well, saying *"you don’t have to wait"* can come across as dismissive or condescending. Some people would rather wait than feel like their time was wasted. - **Flashlight Complaint**: If you *were* shining a light (even accidentally), that’s a clear violation of theater etiquette and would frustrate anyone. ### **Was It a "Weird Couple"?** Probably not. Their reaction was **over-the-top**, but their core complaint was valid: - They felt their movie experience was ruined. - They saw it as a breach of trust (theater not delivering what was expected). - They wanted compensation (free pass), which is a reasonable ask in such cases. Most people wouldn’t have yelled, but many would have been annoyed. The fact that they escalated suggests they took it *very* seriously. ### **What Should Have Happened Instead?** 1. **Don’t Assume Everyone Cares**: Some people *do* wait for credits, some don’t. Instead of announcing it, you could’ve: - **Waited until the theater was empty** before cleaning (if possible). - **Checked the door sheet first**—maybe the other movie wasn’t crowded, and you could’ve prioritized that one. - **If you *had* to say something**, try a softer approach: *"Hey, the credits are rolling—if you’re not waiting for them, you can head out now!"* (Less direct, more neutral.) 2. **Follow Workplace Policies**: Since your manager told you to stop, it’s best to comply. Theaters have reasons for their rules (e.g., avoiding complaints, maintaining a certain experience). 3. **Apologize if Needed**: If you’re in a customer-facing role, sometimes the best response is to acknowledge the issue (without agreeing with it). Example: *"I’m sorry if that came across as rude—I was just trying to help everyone move along. I’ll make sure to be more mindful next time."* ### **Final Verdict: 0.7/1 (Mostly Wrong, But Understandable)** - **Not wrong in intent**, but **wrong in execution** because: - It violated theater etiquette. - It risked alienating customers. - It went against your manager’s guidance. - **The couple wasn’t "weird"**—they had a valid complaint, even if their reaction was extreme. **Lesson:** Customer service isn’t just about efficiency—it’s about *perception*. Even if you’re helping, how you do it matters. Next time, err on the side of subtlety or silence unless absolutely necessary. Would you do it again? Probably not, now that you know the consequences. But if you’re in a theater where it’s *common practice* (some do this), then the risk/reward might change.
